blocks.text: The chapter describes Satan’s binding, the martyrs’ life and reign with Christ for a thousand years, Satan’s later release, and final judgment. It calls the martyrs’ life and reign “the first resurrection” and identifies the lake of fire as “the second death.” The text itself does not settle the later questions readers ask about whether the thousand years and its sequence should be read chronologically or symbolically; interpretations differ.

The gathering of Gog and Magog and the final battle belong to Revelation’s wider reworking of Ezekielian imagery. Rather than treating these scenes as isolated details, readers can recognize them as part of Revelation’s own sequence of throne, plague, battle, city, river, and tree imagery.

sections.title: Questions Raised by the Thousand Years

blocks.text: Across Revelation, the visions repeatedly rework Israel’s Scriptures, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. This broader pattern helps explain why the chapter’s images are densely connected with the book’s larger symbolic world.
